title: Three Homes, Three Lives
intro: You are going to read about three people who live in very different homes.

passage: What does ‘home’ mean to you? For most people, it is a house or a flat. But homes can be very different. We asked three people from three countries to tell us about their homes.

Bolor, 34, lives with her husband and two children in a yurt in the north of Mongolia. ‘Our home is round and made of wood and thick sheep’s wool,’ she says. ‘There is a stove in the middle. We use it for cooking, and it keeps us warm when it is minus thirty outside.’ The family keeps sheep and goats, so they move four times a year to find fresh grass. ‘We can pack the yurt in about two hours and put it on a truck,’ Bolor explains.

Dilshod, 27, is a software engineer in Tashkent. He lives alone on the fourteenth floor of a new building. His flat is small, but it is modern and comfortable. ‘The best thing is the view,’ he says. ‘At night I can see the lights of the whole city.’ But last winter the lift stopped working for a week, and he had to walk up and down the stairs every day. ‘That was good exercise!’ he laughs.

Kate and Sam live on a narrow boat on a canal in London. Rent in the city is very expensive, so six years ago they bought an old boat and repaired it. There isn’t much space inside, and they have very little furniture. In summer, the sound of the rain on the roof is lovely, but in winter the boat can get cold. They must move to a new place on the canal every two weeks, so their neighbours often change.

So, who has the best home? All three are happy with their choice. Bolor loves the open land around her yurt. Dilshod likes living near his office. And Kate says their little boat is the cosiest home in London. ‘It’s small,’ she says, ‘but it’s ours.’
